html:
The Bengal famine of 1943 was a famine in British India during the Second World War. It killed somewhere between 800,000 and 3.8 million people in Bengal and Orissa; about three million is a common estimate. Most died of malaria, cholera and other diseases that hunger made deadly.

Bengal's rural poor were already living on the edge. Rice per person had been falling for decades and many farmers were deep in debt. Then the war hit:

  • Japan took Burma in 1942, cutting off rice imports and putting an army on Bengal's border.
  • Fearing invasion, the British removed boats and rice from coastal districts, a "denial policy" that wrecked fishing and local trade.
  • A cyclone in October 1942 and crop disease cut the harvest.
  • War spending drove prices up, and traders and officials hoarded grain. Bengal's government was slow to admit there was a famine at all.

Starving families sold their land, men left to find work or join the army, and women and children walked to Calcutta looking for food. Relief came late, after the army took charge in late 1943.

How much blame falls on Churchill's war cabinet, which limited grain shipments to India, is still argued. The economist Amartya Sen, who saw the famine as a child, later argued that famines like this come less from a lack of food than from people losing the means to buy it. The famine, like the one in 1770, became part of the case against British rule.
